teacherUse: This is a PUBLIC post-practice solution resource, not teacher-login-secured or an official FBISE marking scheme. Review after collecting student work. Do not treat full-grade blueprint as a Unit 5 quota.
markingPolicy: For each question answer either A or B; award marks only for the chosen option (4 for Section B, 6 for Section C). Accept equivalent scientifically correct method, correct units/rounding and clearly justified reasoning. Never sum both OR choices.
academicStatus: Independent numerical and formula consistency checks are included in CI. Physics teacher must still independently check all wordings, graph assumptions, alternate correct approaches and marks before formal examination use.

marking.text: Newton's second law gives the net force Fnet = ma for constant acceleration.
Use the motion equation v² − u² = 2ad, hence ad = (v² − u²)/2.
Net work Wnet = Fnet d = mad = ½m(v² − u²).
Identify Ki = ½mu² and Kf = ½mv²; therefore Wnet = Kf − Ki = ΔK.

answers.teacherNotes: Assess derivation of ΔK from constant-force motion, not rote recall alone.

marking.text: State the formula K = ½mv² and Wnet = Kf − Ki.
Initial kinetic energy Ki = ½(3.0)(2.0²) = 6.0 J.
Final kinetic energy Kf = ½(3.0)(8.0²) = 96 J.
Net work Wnet = 96 − 6 = +90 J.

answers.teacherNotes: Accept +90 J; a sign explanation may be included with the subtraction.

marking.text: For force component parallel to displacement, work is the signed area under the F∥–x graph.
The force varies linearly; mean force = (4 + 12)/2 = 8 N.
Signed trapezoid area W = mean force × distance = 8 × 6.
Work W = +48 J, positive because the force component stays above the axis.

answers.teacherNotes: The force is explicitly the parallel component, so no extra cosine factor.

marking.text: For linear F∥(x), zero crossing occurs at x = 6 × 8/(8 + 4) = 4.0 m.
Positive triangular area = ½ × 4.0 m × 8 N = +16 J.
Negative triangular area = −½ × 2.0 m × 4 N = −4.0 J.
Total signed work = 16 − 4 = +12 J (not 20 J of unsigned area).

answers.teacherNotes: Credit separate signed areas; adding unsigned areas gives the wrong result.

marking.text: A conservative force does the same work between fixed endpoints regardless of the path taken.
Its net work around any closed path is zero.
Conservative work can be expressed as Wconservative = −ΔU for its potential energy.
A correct example is gravity (also ideal spring or electrostatic force).

answers.teacherNotes: One mark per distinct property; potential-energy sign must be correct.

marking.text: A non-conservative resistive force generally does path-dependent work between the same endpoints.
Kinetic friction opposes displacement, so its work during sliding is negative.
It transfers mechanical energy into other forms, commonly thermal/internal energy.
Kinetic friction or viscous air resistance is a named non-conservative example.

answers.teacherNotes: Friction opposes actual displacement; kinetic energy dissipates into thermal/internal forms.

marking.text: Initial kinetic energy Ki = ½(4.0)(3.0²) = 18 J.
Net work Wnet = (20 − 8) × 4.0 = +48 J.
Final kinetic energy Kf = Ki + Wnet = 18 + 48 = 66 J.
From Kf = ½mv², final speed v = √(2×66/4) = √33 ≈ 5.74 m/s.

answers.teacherNotes: Exact answer √33 m/s or 5.74 m/s at appropriate rounding.

marking.text: Initial kinetic energy Ki = ½(2.0)(6.0²) = 36 J.
Over the proposed 5.0 m, resistance would do Wres = −9.0×5.0 = −45 J; naive target K would be −9 J.
Actual stopping distance is dstop = Ki/9.0 = 36/9 = 4.0 m.
Since dstop < 5.0 m, the body stops after 4.0 m; the proposed 5.0 m is unreachable under the assumptions.

answers.teacherNotes: A negative target K is a reachability warning; do not treat it as an actual final energy.

marking.text: Net work over the straight path: Wnet = Fnet d = 9.0×6.0 = 54 J.
The trolley starts from rest, so its initial kinetic energy is Ki = 0 J.
Work–energy theorem gives final kinetic energy Kf = Ki + Wnet = 54 J.
Solve ½(3.0)v² = 54, yielding v² = 36 and v = 6.0 m/s.

answers.teacherNotes: No extra marks for repeating the same calculation; include rest condition.

marking.text: Kinetic energy is K = ½mv²; its dependence on speed is quadratic.
The ratio Kf/Ki = 100/25 = 4: doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.

answers.teacherNotes: Speed doubling results in a fourfold energy ratio for fixed mass.

marking.text: Positive rectangular area from 0 to 3 m = (+10 N)(3 m) = +30 J.
Negative rectangular area from 3 to 7 m = (−5 N)(4 m) = −20 J.
Net signed work is +30 − 20 = +10 J.
The positive net sign means the specified force does overall positive mechanical work.

answers.teacherNotes: The area below axis contributes negative work; total +10 J.

marking.text: First triangle, 0 to 2 m: W1 = ½×2×8 = +8 J.
Rectangle, 2 to 5 m: W2 = 3×8 = +24 J.
Final triangle, 5 to 7 m: W3 = ½×2×8 = +8 J.
Total work is W = 8 + 24 + 8 = +40 J, all above the displacement axis.

answers.teacherNotes: Students may use decomposition into two triangles and one rectangle.

marking.text: Gravitational work between the same two heights is equal for ramp and staircase routes.
Near Earth's surface Wg = mg(hstart − hend): height difference, not path length, sets the work.
Over a full closed round trip to the starting height, gravity's total work is 0 J.
Path-independent endpoint work and zero closed-loop work define gravity as conservative.

answers.teacherNotes: Distinguish work by gravity from extra applied effort due to friction on different routes.

marking.text: Kinetic friction acts opposite sliding displacement and generally performs negative work.
With constant friction magnitude, Wf = −fkL, so a longer path increases the magnitude of energy loss.
Work by friction converts some mechanical energy to internal/thermal energy.
On a closed rough route friction generally does nonzero negative work; it is non-conservative.

answers.teacherNotes: Closed-path negative friction work is generally nonzero; do not confuse with gravity.

marking.text: Newton's second law for constant net acceleration is Fnet = ma.
The straight-line equation of motion is v² − u² = 2ad.
Rearrange: ad = (v² − u²)/2.
Net work Wnet = Fnet d = mad.
Substituting ad gives Wnet = ½mv² − ½mu² = ΔK.
For motion starting from rest, u=0 so kinetic energy K = ½mv²; this generalises to Wnet=Kf−Ki.

answers.teacherNotes: Any equivalent algebraic sequence with physical assumptions earns marks.

marking.text: First stage net work W1 = F1d1 = 8.0×5.0 = +40 J.
Starting from rest, K1 = 0 + 40 = 40 J.
Speed after stage 1: v1 = √(2K1/m) = √(80/2) = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s.
Second-stage retarding work W2 = −(4.0)(3.0) = −12 J.
After stage 2, final kinetic energy K2 = 40 − 12 = 28 J.

answers.teacherNotes: Two phases: the retarding force does negative work but the body remains moving through 3m.

marking.text: Initial kinetic energy Ki = ½(5.0)(2.0²) = 10 J.
Work done by the applied forward force Wa = (+30)(4.0) = +120 J.
Work done by opposing resistance Wr = (−12)(4.0) = −48 J.
Net work Wnet = Wa + Wr = 120 − 48 = +72 J.
Final kinetic energy Kf = Ki + Wnet = 10 + 72 = 82 J.

answers.teacherNotes: Resistance work is negative; work done against resistance would be positive +48 J.

marking.text: Initial kinetic energy Ki = ½(3.0)(8.0²) = 96 J.
Net forward force Fnet = 5.0 − 17 = −12 N.
Hypothetical work over 10.0 m: Wnet = (−12)(10) = −120 J.
Naively computed Ktarget = 96 − 120 = −24 J, which is not physically possible.
With a 12 N net stopping force, dstop = Ki/12 = 96/12 = 8.0 m.
The body stops at 8.0 m with K = 0; it cannot reach 10.0 m under the assumed constant forces.

answers.teacherNotes: The 10m target is unreachable; final physical energy is zero at the earlier 8m stop.
